title: The god within
hookLine: God is near you, with you, within you (Letters 41)

lines: NONE OF THAT DISTANCE IS NEEDED.
cards: In a Roman temple, it wasn't unusual to see someone ask the temple keeper for a favor: let me get close to the statue, close to its ear, so the god will hear me better. People raised their hands toward the sky to pray.
In the forty-first letter, Seneca tells Lucilius that none of that distance is necessary, and says why in a sentence of three short pieces.

teach.b: In Richard Gummere's 1917 translation: "God is near you, he is with you, he is within you." The Latin is even shorter: prope est a te deus, tecum est, intus est. Near, with, within, each step closer than the last.

teach.h: A HOLY SPIRIT DWELLS IN US.
teach.b: A holy spirit dwells within us, Seneca says, watching our good and bad deeds and guarding us. As we treat it, so it treats us. No one is good without God's help.
It's worth being careful about what Seneca meant by God.
For the Stoics, god was the divine reason running through the whole universe, the same reason that sparks in every human mind.
That's not the same picture as the personal God of Jewish, Christian or Muslim scripture, though people have heard echoes in both directions.
The Christian writer Tertullian called Seneca often one of ours, and later a set of letters claiming to be between Seneca and the apostle Paul circulated; they are not considered genuine.

Why it matters on a Tuesday: if what you're looking for is near, with and within, you don't need a special building, a better connection or a perfect mood to begin. You can turn toward it at a red light.
Whatever name you use, or none, Seneca's claim is that the distance is shorter than it seems.

how: Some people repeat Seneca's 'near, with, within' as a short reflection during the day; some religious readers hear it alongside their own scripture's teaching that God is close.

o: a sacred spirit within us that watches and guards us
the breath that keeps the body alive from day to day
a god who lives far off, above the clouds and sky

games.q: the god within — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca tells Lucilius to get close to the statue's ear
he says there's no need: God is near, with, within.
the letters between Seneca and the apostle Paul are genuine

games.q: you're in a Roman temple. people are asking the keeper to let them near the statue's ear. what does Seneca say?
o: get as close to the statue as you can.
God is near you, with you, within you.
shout, so the god can hear.
games.why: Seneca says there's no need to raise hands to the sky or reach the idol's ear: the divine is already within.

practice: Let your breathing slow, and take Seneca's three words one at a time, whatever they mean to you: near on one out-breath, with on the next, within on the next.
You don't need to believe anything particular to sit with the thought that what matters most isn't far away. If you pray, let the words lead into your own prayer.
